 Court of Appeal upholds URA's Shs270m tax deduction from ex-Spinning Mills workers
Friday, October 30, 2026

 By  
 Juliet Kigongo 
 Summary 
 Article

What you need to know:
 Addressing procedural concerns, the appellate judges noted that URA became an indispensable party to the suit once the tax authority received the withheld funds, directly impacting its financial mandate. While the panel faulted the High Court judge for failing to issue rulings on preliminary objections raised by URA, they concluded that the oversight did not cause a miscarriage of justice or invalidate the application.
 The Court of Appeal has upheld the decision by the Uganda Revenue Authority (URA) to deduct Shs269.6 million in Pay As You Earn (PAYE) tax from the terminal benefits of more than 1,400 former employees of the defunct Uganda Spinning Mills Limited (USML), reversing an earlier High Court order that had mandated a full refund with interest.
 In a unanimous decision, a three-justice panel comprising Deputy Chief Justice Moses Kazibwe Kawumi, Justice Cheborion Barishaki, and Justice Asa Mugenyi ruled that terminal benefits paid to former employees constitute taxable income under the Income Tax Act, regardless of whether the beneficiaries have already severed employment ties.
The justices set aside the 2016 High Court ruling that had declared the tax deductions unlawful and directed URA and the Attorney General to refund the money to the former staff.
 Writing the lead judgment, Justice Barishaki noted that while the High Court judge correctly followed the law as it stood at the time of his ruling, a landmark Supreme Court decision delivered on December 20, 2017—in the case of URA versus Siraje Hassan Kajura—fundamentally altered the legal landscape. The apex court held that terminal packages are compensation arising from employment and are taxable under Section 19(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act.
 "It is now settled law that terminal benefits are taxable income," Justice Barishaki ruled, emphasizing that the Supreme Court's binding precedent applies retroactively to all pending matters. "An employment benefit remains taxable even where it is paid to someone who has already left employment, provided it arose from their past employment."
 Justice Barishaki added, "The terminal benefits paid to the respondents, the former employees of the defunct Uganda Spinning Mills Ltd, were lawfully taxed in the form of PAYE."
The protracted legal dispute originated from a consent judgment in the High Court, under which the government agreed to pay the former workers a total of Shs4.98 billion following the privatization and closure of the Lira-based textile manufacturer in 2002.
However, during the disbursement process, the Privatisation Unit and the Attorney General recomputed the packages and withheld Shs269.6 million as PAYE tax, remitting it directly to URA. Consequently, the former employees received a net payout of Shs4.71 billion.
 Dissatisfied with the reduced payout, the former workers successfully challenged the deduction in September 2016, with the High Court ordering URA and the state to refund the money alongside a 24 percent annual interest rate. URA and the Attorney General subsequently appealed, arguing that the High Court relied on an outdated Court of Appeal ruling that was later overturned by the apex court.
 Addressing procedural concerns, the appellate judges noted that URA became an indispensable party to the suit once the tax authority received the withheld funds, directly impacting its financial mandate. While the panel faulted the High Court judge for failing to issue rulings on preliminary objections raised by URA, they concluded that the oversight did not cause a miscarriage of justice or invalidate the application.
 Concluding the legal battle, the Court of Appeal confirmed that the Shs269.6 million tax deduction was executed strictly in accordance with the law. The court ordered each party to bear its own legal costs for both the High Court and Court of Appeal proceedings, observing that all parties had acted based on legal precedents that were subsequently altered by the Supreme Court.
